newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Labour's Cullen says RBNZ must let currency fall.
newsitem.headline: Labour's Cullen says RBNZ must let currency fall.

text.p: Labour Party finance spokesman Michael Cullen said on Thursday the Reserve Bank must allow the New Zealand dollar to fall.

In a strongly-worded statement, Cullen said: "What is needed is a clear statement from the Reserve Bank that it will stop turning speculation on the New Zealand dollar into a one-sided bet. It must be made abundantly clear that the exchange rate will be allowed to fall to a more natural level."
Labour and the caretaker National Party government are both in negotiations with nationalist New Zealand First to form a government after last month's general election.

Cullen said: "The Reserve Bank needs to state that it is prepared to see interest rates drop sufficiently to allow the exchange rate to be rebalanced. As long as that statement is not forthcoming, those trading in the exchange market are protected against loss on the New Zealand dollar. And that merely seems to entrench its excessive value."
New Zealand First also argues the currency is overvalued.
Cullen said it was illogical and unjust to suggest that interest rates and the exchange rate would have to be pushed up even further unless the government accumulated ever larger fiscal surpluses.
He said a "coordinated propaganda" campaign was being waged against increases in spending in areas like health and education, as proposed by Labour.

On Monday, Reserve Bank Governor Don Brash urged spending restraint to curtail the New Zealand dollar and said parties to coalition talks may have to rethink the second round of a NZ$3 billion tax cut package due in mid-1997.
Cullen said the poor, the sick and children should not have to bear "the burden of the failure of monetary policy to maintain a realistic exchange rate".
He said no one was proposing to run fiscal deficits.

"The real problem is with the operation of monetary policy, and it is this which must change. New Zealand is running the most unbalanced mix of exchange rates, interest rates, fiscal surpluses and current account deficits in the developed world."

Cullen said strong fiscal surpluses over the last year had still seen a rising exchange rate and a deteriorating current account. "They are clearly not the answer as long as monetary policy is operated in such an unbalanced fashion," he said.
